passage:
The common law tradition has long treated indigenous land rights as a species of property right, subject to the same frameworks of alienability, exclusivity, and continuous occupation that govern all real property. Courts applying this tradition typically examine documentary evidence—deeds, surveys, colonial grants—to determine whether an indigenous community's claim satisfies criteria developed for sedentary agricultural societies. Where indigenous communities cannot produce such documentation, their claims have frequently been extinguished as legally insufficient, even when the communities in question had maintained uninterrupted physical presence on and stewardship of the land for centuries.

This approach, however, misunderstands the nature of indigenous legal traditions. In many of these traditions, land is not an alienable commodity held by discrete individuals but a relational obligation sustained by the community as a whole. Customary stewardship practices—seasonal rotation, ceremonial maintenance, collective harvesting protocols—constitute, within these frameworks, the very exercise of sovereign authority over territory. To demand proof of possession through the lens of Anglo-European conveyancing law is, in effect, to render indigenous sovereignty invisible by the definitional terms of the very legal system claiming to adjudicate it. Courts that have been most attentive to this difficulty have moved toward recognizing oral testimony, customary-law expert evidence, and the internal logic of indigenous governance structures as admissible grounds for territorial claims.
comparativeBPassage:
A widely held view among legal scholars maintains that the accommodation of indigenous land claims within state legal systems requires a fundamental reconceptualization of property—one that displaces the traditional bundle-of-rights model with relational or communitarian alternatives. While the instinct toward accommodation is laudable, this view mistakes the diagnosis for the cure.

Indigenous land claims can be recognized under existing common-law frameworks without abandoning the conceptual architecture of property law. The doctrine of aboriginal title, as developed by courts in Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, already provides a workable mechanism: title may be established by showing that the claimant group occupied the land at the time of Crown sovereignty and that occupation has continued to the present. Continuity of occupation does not require the kind of intensive cultivation or sedentary settlement that critics allege; courts have repeatedly held that seasonal patterns of use, collective stewardship, and governance through customary norms all satisfy the occupation requirement. The framework is not a Procrustean bed but an evolving one, capable of absorbing the evidence that indigenous communities can actually produce.

The deeper risk of wholesale reconceptualization is that it may produce legal uncertainty that disadvantages the very communities it purports to protect. Stable, predictable property frameworks facilitate the long-term resource planning that indigenous communities—like all communities—require. A shift to purely relational concepts, however philosophically coherent, risks consigning indigenous land rights to an ad hoc jurisprudence that leaves them vulnerable to shifting judicial sympathies.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is most central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Should indigenous communities be required to produce documentary evidence in order to establish territorial claims?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Can existing common-law property frameworks adequately recognize indigenous land rights, or must those frameworks be fundamentally reconceived?

choices.label: C
choices.text: What practical procedures should courts follow when evaluating oral testimony offered by indigenous claimants?

choices.label: D
choices.text: How have colonial land grants historically affected the territorial sovereignty of indigenous communities?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Is the doctrine of aboriginal title consistent with the constitutional arrangements of common-law nations?

explanations.correct: Passage A argues that the common-law property framework is structurally incapable of recognizing indigenous sovereignty and that courts must turn to indigenous legal traditions themselves. Passage B contends that existing frameworks—specifically aboriginal title doctrine—are adequate and that wholesale reconceptualization is unnecessary and risky. Both passages are organized around precisely this question.
explanations.A: Passage A raises the documentary-evidence problem, but this is a subsidiary illustration of the deeper adequacy question, not the central question of both passages. Passage B does not focus on document requirements.
explanations.C: Passage A mentions oral testimony as one admissible ground; neither passage addresses the procedural mechanics of evaluating it. This is too narrow and too procedural.
explanations.D: Colonial land grants appear only as a passing example in passage A; passage B does not address them at all.
explanations.E: Constitutional consistency is never addressed by either passage; this choice imports a topic outside the scope of both texts.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree about which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: whether indigenous communities historically exercised forms of governance over their territories

choices.label: B
choices.text: whether courts in common-law jurisdictions have ever recognized seasonal land-use patterns as satisfying occupation requirements

choices.label: C
choices.text: whether the common-law property framework, as currently constituted, is capable of fully recognizing indigenous territorial authority

choices.label: D
choices.text: whether indigenous land rights are best understood as communal rather than individual entitlements

choices.label: E
choices.text: whether legal uncertainty poses risks for communities seeking to plan long-term resource use

explanations.correct: Passage A's central argument is that the common-law framework is structurally deficient—it renders indigenous sovereignty invisible by design—and that meaningful recognition requires engaging indigenous legal traditions on their own terms. Passage B argues that the framework is already adequate: aboriginal title doctrine, properly interpreted, can absorb indigenous evidence and governance norms. This is the precise point of disagreement.
explanations.A: Neither author disputes that indigenous communities exercised governance over their territories; passage B explicitly invokes 'governance through customary norms' as sufficient for the occupation requirement.
explanations.B: Both passages accept this. Passage A notes that courts attentive to the problem have expanded admissible evidence; passage B states that courts have 'repeatedly held' seasonal use satisfies occupation. They agree on this fact.
explanations.D: Both passages treat indigenous land rights as communal; passage B's aboriginal title framework applies to 'claimant groups,' not individuals. Neither disputes the communal character.
explanations.E: Both authors accept that legal uncertainty is harmful to communities—passage B raises it as a risk of reconceptualization, and passage A's concern about extinguished claims implies a desire for stable recognition, not instability.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A advocates abandoning common-law property doctrine entirely, while passage B defends that doctrine without qualification.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A diagnoses a structural failure in the common-law treatment of indigenous land claims and advocates engaging indigenous legal frameworks; passage B concedes the failure but argues that an internal reform of existing doctrine is preferable to wholesale reconceptualization.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A presents an empirical survey of court decisions denying indigenous land claims; passage B offers a theoretical defense of aboriginal title doctrine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A and passage B both argue that indigenous land rights should be recognized under common-law frameworks, differing only on the evidentiary standards courts should apply.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A describes indigenous governance practices that common-law courts cannot assess; passage B argues that those same practices fall outside the scope of any legal system.

explanations.correct: Passage A diagnoses common-law property frameworks as structurally incapable of recognizing indigenous sovereignty and calls for engagement with indigenous legal traditions on their own terms. Passage B agrees that there is a problem with naive application of standard property criteria but argues that the aboriginal title doctrine already provides an adequate internal solution, making reconceptualization unnecessary and risky. This is a classic 'diagnosis agreed, cure disputed' structure.
explanations.A: Passage A does not advocate abandoning common-law doctrine entirely; it calls for courts to recognize oral testimony and customary law within legal proceedings. Passage B qualifies its defense of existing doctrine by acknowledging the need for an 'evolving' framework, not an unqualified one.
explanations.C: Neither passage is an empirical survey of court decisions. Both make normative arguments illustrated by selective examples.
explanations.D: Passage A does not argue that indigenous rights should be recognized under common-law frameworks as they currently stand; it argues that those frameworks are inadequate. The two passages differ not merely on evidentiary standards but on the adequacy of the framework itself.
explanations.E: Passage B explicitly argues that indigenous governance practices can be assessed under aboriginal title doctrine; passage A does not claim they fall beyond the reach of any legal system—it argues they fall beyond the reach of the common-law framework as conventionally applied.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A as a requirement for establishing indigenous land claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: evidence that the claimant group maintained collective harvesting protocols

choices.label: B
choices.text: recognition of customary stewardship practices as exercises of sovereign authority

choices.label: C
choices.text: a showing that the claimant group's occupation of the land predates the assertion of Crown sovereignty

choices.label: D
choices.text: the use of oral testimony as admissible evidence before the court

choices.label: E
choices.text: expert evidence concerning the internal logic of indigenous governance structures

explanations.correct: Passage B specifies that aboriginal title requires showing occupation 'at the time of Crown sovereignty'—the temporal anchor to Crown assertion. Passage A discusses occupation and stewardship generally but never introduces Crown sovereignty as the relevant baseline date. This requirement appears only in passage B.
explanations.A: Collective harvesting protocols are mentioned in passage A as an example of customary stewardship practice; passage B does not use this specific phrase.
explanations.B: The characterization of stewardship practices as exercises of sovereign authority appears in passage A, not passage B.
explanations.D: Oral testimony is mentioned in passage A as one of the grounds toward which attentive courts have moved; passage B does not specifically mention oral testimony.
explanations.E: Expert evidence concerning indigenous governance structures is mentioned in passage A; passage B refers to governance through customary norms as satisfying the occupation requirement but does not mention expert witnesses.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from passage A that the author would most likely regard which one of the following as evidence that a court had adequately addressed the problem the author identifies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court rules in favor of an indigenous claimant after finding that the group held a deed predating colonial occupation of the territory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court extinguishes an indigenous land claim after determining that the group could not demonstrate continuous sedentary settlement on the land.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court recognizes an indigenous community's territorial authority on the basis of expert testimony describing the community's customary governance protocols and seasonal land-use cycles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legislature enacts a statute requiring all indigenous land claims to be evaluated under the same property criteria applied to non-indigenous claimants.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court defers a ruling on an indigenous land claim pending the production of eighteenth-century survey records by the claimant community.

explanations.correct: Passage A explicitly endorses courts that 'have moved toward recognizing oral testimony, customary-law expert evidence, and the internal logic of indigenous governance structures as admissible grounds for territorial claims.' A court recognizing territorial authority on the basis of customary governance expert testimony and seasonal land-use cycles is precisely the example passage A holds up as the corrective to the structural failure it diagnoses.
explanations.A: A deed is exactly the kind of documentary evidence passage A identifies as the inadequate, Eurocentric standard; a ruling that succeeds because of a deed does not address the structural problem passage A describes.
explanations.B: Demanding continuous sedentary settlement is the very criterion passage A identifies as structurally biased against indigenous communities—a court applying that criterion exemplifies the problem, not a solution.
explanations.D: Applying the same property criteria to indigenous and non-indigenous claimants is what passage A criticizes; uniform application of Anglo-European conveyancing law renders indigenous sovereignty invisible.
explanations.E: Deferring a claim pending the production of eighteenth-century survey records replicates the documentary-evidence demand that passage A identifies as the source of extinguishment; this is the problem, not the remedy.

questions.questionStem: In passage B, the reference to the doctrine of aboriginal title as 'not a Procrustean bed but an evolving one' functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: acknowledge that the doctrine has historically disadvantaged indigenous claimants while arguing that this history is irrelevant to its current application

choices.label: B
choices.text: concede that the doctrine contains rigid elements while maintaining that those elements cannot be modified through judicial interpretation

choices.label: C
choices.text: counter the objection that existing common-law frameworks are inherently ill-suited to indigenous evidence by characterizing the doctrine as flexible and adaptable

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the aboriginal title doctrine with other common-law property frameworks that passage B regards as genuinely inflexible

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce the author's proposal that courts formally adopt a new standard for evaluating indigenous governance evidence

explanations.correct: The Procrustean-bed metaphor directly answers the critic (implicit in passage A and the scholarly view passage B opens by engaging) who holds that the common-law framework is a rigid, ill-fitting structure that forces indigenous claims into categories that distort or erase them. By calling the doctrine 'not a Procrustean bed but an evolving one,' passage B rebuts that charge: the framework is capacious and adaptive, not rigid. The sentence thus serves as the rhetorical pivot in B's defense of existing doctrine.
explanations.A: Passage B does not concede that the doctrine has historically disadvantaged indigenous claimants, nor does it argue that history is irrelevant. The phrase does not perform this function.
explanations.B: Calling the framework 'evolving' is the opposite of conceding its elements are unmodifiable through judicial interpretation; the phrase implies courts have already been adapting it.
explanations.D: Passage B does not contrast aboriginal title with other common-law frameworks or suggest any other framework is less flexible. No other property doctrine is mentioned in the passage.
explanations.E: Passage B does not propose a new formal standard; it argues that the existing doctrine, properly understood, is adequate. The passage advocates interpretation, not legislative or doctrinal innovation.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage A would be most likely to make which one of the following criticisms of the argument advanced in passage B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage B incorrectly assumes that indigenous communities in Canada, Australia, and New Zealand share a uniform set of customary land-use practices.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage B's invocation of the aboriginal title doctrine does not resolve the underlying problem because that doctrine still evaluates indigenous claims by criteria—occupation, continuity, Crown-sovereignty baseline—whose meaning is defined by the very framework that passage A identifies as structurally inadequate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage B overstates the degree of legal certainty that the aboriginal title doctrine has provided to indigenous communities in practice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage B ignores the importance of legislative rather than judicial solutions to the problem of indigenous land rights.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage B's concern about ad hoc jurisprudence is misplaced because indigenous communities do not actually rely on property frameworks for long-term resource planning.

explanations.correct: Passage A's central claim is that demanding proof through Anglo-European legal criteria renders indigenous sovereignty invisible by the definitional terms of the adjudicating system itself. Passage B's response invokes aboriginal title, which measures occupation, continuity, and a Crown-sovereignty baseline—all terms whose content is determined by common-law courts applying common-law concepts. The author of passage A would argue that this is precisely the circularity identified in passage A: the framework evaluates indigenous claims using criteria defined by the framework being challenged, so the 'evolution' passage B celebrates is still bounded by the same definitional horizon.
explanations.A: Passage A never argues that indigenous land practices are uniform; its argument is structural, not ethnographic. Uniformity across jurisdictions is not a premise of passage A, so this would not be a criticism the author of passage A would make.
explanations.C: Passage A does not discuss the empirical track record of aboriginal title litigation or levels of certainty it has provided. Passage A's objection is structural-conceptual, not empirical-historical.
explanations.D: Neither passage addresses the legislature-versus-judiciary question. Passage A advocates judicial recognition of indigenous legal traditions; it does not argue that legislative solutions are preferable.
explanations.E: Passage A does not make any claim about how indigenous communities conduct long-term resource planning; disputing that claim is outside the scope of passage A's argument and would not be a criticism the author of passage A would voice.
